questions.q: What is the full form of EPR in the context of India's E-Waste Management Rules, and what is its core obligation for producers?
questions.a: EPR stands for Extended Producer Responsibility. Its core obligation: producers (manufacturers, importers, brand owners) are financially and physically responsible for the collection, recycling, and environmentally sound disposal of their products after end-of-life. A wrong answer (e.g., "Electronic Product Recycling" or "producers only pay a tax") reveals confusion between EPR and a simple tax/fee model — EPR requires operational take-back systems, not just monetary payment.

questions.q: A student says: "E-waste is just plastic and metal — it's not dangerous like chemical waste." Explain why this statement is incorrect using three specific toxic substances found in e-waste and their targeted health effects.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect because e-waste contains concentrated hazardous substances: (1) Lead in solder/CRT glass — causes neurological damage, especially in children; (2) Mercury in switches/flat-panel displays — impairs brain/kidney function; (3) Cadmium in Ni-Cd batteries/semiconductors — causes kidney failure and bone disease (itai-itai). A wrong answer that only mentions "pollution" or "heavy metals" without naming specific substance→effect pairs shows superficial awareness, not mechanistic understanding of toxicity pathways.

questions.q: Your household has generated 5 kg of mixed e-waste (old router, two feature phones, laptop battery, assorted cables). Step-by-step, describe how you would prepare and dispose of this e-waste responsibly in an Indian metro city, referencing at least one government portal.
questions.a: Steps: (1) Segregate: separate battery (lithium-ion) from other items — tape battery terminals to prevent short-circuit. (2) Data sanitization: factory-reset phones, wipe laptop drive (use DBAN or built-in reset). (3) Locate authorized recycler: visit cpcb.nic.in → "E-Waste" → "List of Authorized Recyclers/Dismantlers" for your state/city. (4) Contact recycler: confirm acceptance of mixed e-waste, schedule pickup or drop-off. (5) Obtain acknowledgment: request Form-6 (certificate of recycling) for records. A wrong answer that suggests "give to kabadiwala" or "dump in blue bin" reveals ignorance of formal channel requirements and data security risks.

questions.q: Compare the environmental impact of informal sector recycling (open burning, acid leaching) vs. formal sector recycling (mechanical shredding, hydrometallurgy) for a printed circuit board (PCB). Which recovers more gold per tonne, and why does the informal sector persist despite lower recovery?
questions.a: Formal recycling recovers >95% of gold (≈300 g/tonne PCB) via controlled hydrometallurgy; informal acid leaching recovers <30% and releases cyanide/acid effluents. Informal sector persists due to: (a) lower operational cost (no pollution controls), (b) doorstep collection convenience for households, (c) lack of awareness about authorized channels, (d) economic necessity for unskilled workers. A wrong answer claiming "informal recovers more gold because they use strong acid" confuses reagent strength with process control — uncontrolled acid leaching dissolves gold but fails to precipitate it efficiently, losing most to waste sludge.

questions.q: Critique this school e-waste drive plan: "Students bring all old electronics from home; we pile them in the courtyard; a local scrap dealer offers ₹50/kg and takes everything away." Identify three violations of E-Waste Management Rules 2022 and propose a compliant alternative.
questions.a: Violations: (1) Handing e-waste to unauthorized scrap dealer (Rule 9: only authorized dismantlers/recyclers). (2) No data sanitization — risk of student data breach. (3) Open storage in courtyard — exposure to rain/heat accelerates toxin leaching. Compliant alternative: Partner with a CPCB-authorized recycler for a scheduled pickup; conduct a data-wiping workshop beforehand; store e-waste in covered, labeled bins; obtain Form-6 certificates for school records. A wrong answer focusing only on "money lost" misses the legal and ecological core of the violation.

questions.q: Design a 4-week community e-waste awareness campaign for a residential society (200 flats). Include: (a) one quantitative target, (b) two behavior-change nudges, (c) one partnership with a formal entity, and (d) a metric to evaluate long-term impact.
questions.a: Campaign: "E-Waste Warriors". (a) Target: Collect 500 kg e-waste in 4 weeks (2.5 kg/flat). (b) Nudges: (i) "Green Bin" at each tower entrance with QR code linking to recycler pickup schedule (reduces friction); (ii) Monthly "Zero E-Waste Home" badge displayed on society app (social proof). (c) Partnership: MoU with CPCB-authorized recycler for monthly pickup + Form-6 issuance. (d) Long-term metric: % of flats using authorized channel in subsequent 6 months (tracked via recycler logs). A poor answer lacking specific nudges or formal partnership shows inability to translate awareness into systemic change.
